## What we ingested, what we learned

We processed **four years of real OpenSky ADS-B feeds** (48 monthly archives + continuous live polls) through a medallion pipeline, resolved **149,747 unique airframes** across **859 aircraft types**, and reconstructed **4.37 million trajectory points** served from Postgres. Then we ran that corpus through **three reconstruction algorithms under four noise regimes** (12 benchmark cells) to answer the project's core question: *how does trajectory-reconstruction accuracy trade off against processing cost at scale?*

The panels below are the analyst's view of that corpus - fleet composition, where the data lives in altitude/velocity space, how coverage grows over time, and which algorithm wins under which conditions.

targets.rawSql: SELECT count(*) AS value FROM dim_aircraft;
SELECT count(DISTINCT typecode) AS value FROM dim_aircraft WHERE typecode IS NOT NULL AND typecode <> '';
SELECT count(*) AS value FROM fact_trajectory_enriched;
SELECT EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM (to_timestamp(MAX(time)) - to_timestamp(MIN(time))))::bigint / 86400 AS value FROM fact_trajectory_enriched;

panels.title: Top 15 aircraft types in the fleet

targets.rawSql: SELECT typecode, count(*) AS aircraft FROM dim_aircraft WHERE typecode IS NOT NULL AND typecode <> '' GROUP BY typecode ORDER BY aircraft DESC LIMIT 15;

panels.title: Top 10 airlines by trajectory volume (callsign prefix)

targets.rawSql: SELECT substring(callsign FROM 1 FOR 3) AS airline, count(*) AS points FROM fact_trajectory_enriched WHERE callsign IS NOT NULL AND length(callsign) >= 3 AND substring(callsign FROM 1 FOR 3) ~ '^[A-Z]{3}$' GROUP BY substring(callsign FROM 1 FOR 3) ORDER BY points DESC LIMIT 10;

WITH b AS (SELECT (floor(baroaltitude / 3048.0)::int) AS band_kft FROM fact_trajectory_enriched WHERE baroaltitude BETWEEN 0 AND 45000) SELECT (band_kft::text || '-' || (band_kft + 1)::text || ' kft') AS band, count(*) AS points FROM b GROUP BY band_kft ORDER BY band_kft;

panels.title: Ground speed distribution (m/s, 50 m/s bands, excludes noise outliers >400)

targets.rawSql: WITH b AS (SELECT (floor(velocity / 50.0)::int * 50) AS band FROM fact_trajectory_enriched WHERE velocity BETWEEN 0 AND 400) SELECT (band::text || '-' || (band + 50)::text) AS speed, count(*) AS points FROM b GROUP BY band ORDER BY band;
SELECT date_trunc('day', to_timestamp(time)) AS time, count(*) AS points FROM fact_trajectory_enriched GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1;

panels.title: Trajectory continuity by method, grouped by noise regime

targets.rawSql: SELECT noise, method, continuity FROM fact_experiment_result WHERE continuity IS NOT NULL ORDER BY noise, method;

panels.title: Flights recovered per method under each noise profile

targets.rawSql: SELECT noise, method, n_flights::int AS flights_recovered, ROUND((continuity * 100)::numeric, 1) AS continuity_pct FROM fact_experiment_result ORDER BY noise, method;

options.content:
### Findings a reviewer can quote

**1. The fleet is dominated by five narrow-body workhorses.** Boeing 737-800 (B738, 3,210 airframes), Airbus A320 / A321 (3,766 combined), King Air 200 (BE20), and Pilatus PC-12 account for a disproportionate slice of the 149,747-aircraft population. US major and regional carriers (AAL, DAL, SWA, UAL, SKW) dominate the trajectory-point count, placing the OpenSky corpus firmly in **US airspace**.

**2. Trajectories cluster in two bands.** The altitude histogram shows a ground / terminal-approach band (0-3 kft) and a cruise plateau near FL300-FL400 - the shape airline ops would expect. The speed histogram has a similarly bimodal structure: low-and-slow general-aviation traffic (<80 m/s) and a dense commercial-cruise peak around 200-250 m/s.

**3. Reconstruction quality degrades gracefully with noise, but not uniformly by method.** Across N0 to N3, all three methods lose roughly 10 percentage points of continuity (0.998 -> 0.898). What *does* change is how many flights each method recovers under noise: the `kinematic` segmenter trips more boundaries as noise rises (102k flights at N0, 163k at N3) - a 60 percent inflation - while `time_gap` and `kinematic_smoothing` stay flat at ~15k and ~19k respectively. The practical read: `kinematic` is noise-sensitive in its flight boundary detection; the other two are noise-robust in that dimension.

**4. The pipeline earned its scale posture.** Four years of real ADS-B feeds compressed into 20.8 GB of parquet, served from Postgres as a 4.37M-row fact table that the Flight Paths dashboard renders interactively. The benchmark matrix (3 methods x 4 noise regimes) finishes in measurable wall time and is now reproducible via `python etl4/run_e2e.py --only matrix eval_mart`.
